Levodopa-responsive progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus associated with 
glycine receptor antibodies  
ARTICLE INFO  
Keywords 
PERM syndrome 
Autoimmune encephalitis 
Pathogenesis  
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM) 
syndrome is a rare autoimmune encephalitis, often associated with 
glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), dipeptidyl-peptidase – like protein 6 
(DPPX), or glycine receptors (GlyR) antibodies [ 1 ]. The most relevant 
features of PERM syndrome are rigidity, myoclonus, dysautonomia, and 
brainstem dysfunction [ 1 ]. Symptoms during the acute phase can be 
severe, and response to immunotherapy variable [ 1 ]. We report a case of 
PERM syndrome with poor response to immunotherapy in which levo -
dopa resulted in marked clinical improvement, facilitating his subse -
quent rehabilitation. 
This 41-year-old man with prior history of hepatitis C acutely 
developed dizziness, headache, and vomiting. A diagnosis of peripheral 
vestibular syndrome was made during an emergency evaluation. 
Recrudescence of vertigo, new left facial nerve palsy, and progressive 
respiratory distress evolved on the next day, requiring admission in the 
intensive care unit (ICU) for endotracheal intubation. Over the next few 
days, he manifested fixed limbs rigidity, episodes of generalized myoc -
lonus, bilateral ptosis (prevalent in the right eye), persistent right gaze 
deviation, dysphagia, drowsiness, nystagmus, and dysautonomic fea -
tures (neurogenic bladder and hypertension). Routine laboratory in -
vestigations, including the search for onconeural antibodies with a 
commercial test (Euroimmun, Lubeck, Germany), electroencephalog -
raphy, and brain MRI were unremarkable. Lumbar puncture showed 
intrathecal IgG synthesis (IgG-index = 0.8; unique-to-CSF oligoclonal 
IgG bands). Treatment with high-dose steroids was followed by intra -
venous immunoglobulin with only respiratory function improvement, 
sufficient to interrupt mechanical ventilation but without motor 
improvement. He was discharged from ICU after 3 months and trans -
ferred to a rehabilitation center. However, physical therapy was 
hampered due to the persistence of severe rigidity, compounded by 
intermittent axial hypotonia ( Video 1 , online) due to weakness of neck 
flexor muscles. 
Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi. 
org/10.1016/j.parkreldis.2020.11.008 
The combination of axial hypotonia, limbs rigidity, and oculomotor 
dysfunction is common in childhood dopa-responsive disorders due to 
selected disruptions in the dopamine metabolism pathways. Therefore, 
after 4 months of unsuccessful rehabilitation and unresponsiveness to 
GABAergic drugs (baclofen, clonazepam), he was treated with low doses 
of levodopa/benserazide up to 300/75 mg/daily, with marked 
improvement in rigidity and axial hypotonia within a week ( Video 2 , 
online). It was at this stage that GlyR antibodies were identified in serum 
and CSF using an in-house live cell-based assay [ 1 ]. A levodopa taper led 
to the reemergence of severe rigidity, promptly corrected when levo -
dopa was restarted. After 10 months of rehabilitation while on levodopa, 
the patient achieved symptom resolution except for the presence of mild

neurogenic bladder ( Video 3 , online). He has remained clinically stable 
with levodopa after 24 months follow-up, despite persistent GlyR anti -
bodies in serum. A DATscan obtained at this stage was normal (unable to 
obtain previously given his critical condition and inability to tolerate 
such procedure). The absence of hepatitis C-associated cancers or 
autoimmune conditions was confirmed at this stage. This case prompted 
a review of the literature, showing a variety of clinical features in GlyR 
antibody-associated disorders, including parkinsonism and other extra -
pyramidal features [ 2 ] ( Table 1 ; Supplementary material 1). 
Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi. 
org/10.1016/j.parkreldis.2020.11.008 
GlyR antibody-associated PERM syndrome is a rare disorder that can 
be life-threatening if not treated ( Table 1 ). In our patients, the recovery 
was delayed due to insufficient benefit from immunomodulatory treat -
ments, which was only facilitated by the high response to levodopa. The 
combination of limbs rigidity and axial hypotonia is a well-known 
combination of the hypodopaminergic childhood-onset dopa-respon -
sive disorders due to tyrosine hydroxylase [ 3 ] or sepiapterin reductase 
deficiencies [ 4 ]. Such syndromic ascertainment was further supported 
by the presence of ptosis and sustained right gaze, a feature that could 
have well been characterized as oculogyric crisis [ 5 ]. 
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first case of GlyR antibody- 
associated PERM manifested by levodopa responsive axial hypotonia 
and oculomotor abnormalities, suggesting an interaction between GlyR 
antibodies and motor control networks. GlyRs have been identified in 
the striatum, globus pallidus, and substantia nigra (both pars compacta 
and reticulata), showing an increase of dopamine release after glycine 
application [ 6 ]. As a result, dopamine supply in both the direct and 
indirect pathways could have been reduced in the presence of GlyR 
antibodies, given the disruption of the glycinergic neurotransmission 
mediated by GlyR antibodies [ 7 ]. The exacerbation of rigidity after a few 
hours of levodopa discontinuation with rapid improvement upon reex -
posure supports the efficacy of this treatment in our patient. Although it 
was not performed in the acute phase of the disease, our patient ’ s

have been in response to functional abnormalities caused by the anti -
bodies, rather than from underlying dopaminergic neuronal loss. 
In conclusion, this case expands the phenotypic spectrum of GlyR 
antibody-associated PERM, including dopa-responsive abnormalities. 
The exquisite response to levodopa markedly facilitated the rehabilita -
tion efforts required for maximizing functional recovery.
